Testimony of Rep. Adam Lee presenting
LD 347, An Act to Provide Qualifying Municipalities a Percentage of Adult
Use Cannabis Sales Tax and Excise Tax Revenue
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Veterans and Legal Affairs
Senator Hickman, Representative Supica and distinguished members of the Joint Standing
Committee on Veterans and Legal Affairs, I am Adam Lee, and I represent House District 89 which is Downtown Auburn and New Auburn. I'm here to introduce LD 347, An Act to Provide
Qualifying Municipalities a Percentage of Adult Use Cannabis Sales Tax and Excise Tax
Revenue.
LD 347 proposes to provide municipalities 12% of the revenue from the sales and excise taxes
on adult use cannabis and cannabis products. To be clear, this bill does not in any way alter the
amount of taxes assessed on these products. This allocation represents a thoughtful balance between state revenue needs and local municipal support.
I've brought this bill because it honors an important component of the original referendum vote that occurred in 2016, that municipalities that opted into the sale of adult-use cannabis would receive a portion of the proceeds of the tax on sales of those products. I remember this component. I was a City Councilor at the time in Auburn. This aspect of the referendum was
essential to my vote and my support for it. Auburn has embraced this industry. As a consequence
of the legislature's actions obviating this portion of the proposed referendum statute, it has received very little in return for its embrace of the industry.
This revenue is particularly important for our municipalities to defray the expenses caused by the embrace of the industry. These expenses often include additional administrative costs, zoning
modifications and enhanced public safety measures that many of our towns and cities have had
to implement.
The proposed 12% revenue share represents a carefully considered approach that acknowledges
the significant responsibilities and costs borne by our local governments.

District 89: Part of Auburn

I respectfully ask the committee to support LD 347. This legislation will create a more equitable
framework for carmabis revenue sharing while ensuring our communities have the resources they need to manage this growing industry properly.
Thank you for your consideration. I would be happy to answer any questions you may have.
District 89: Part of Auburn
10032845:
Maine Mayors Coalition Testimony on LD 177, An Act to Create Municipal Cannabis Revenue Sharing, and LD 347, An Act to Provide Qualifying Municipalities a Percentage of Adult Use
Cannabis Sales Tax and Excise Tax Revenue
Senator Hickman, Representative Supica and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Veterans and Legal Affairs, the Maine Mayors Coalition is providing testimony in support of LD 177, An Act to Create Municipal Cannabis Revenue Sharing, and LD 347, An Act to Provide Qualifying Municipalities a Percentage of Adult Use Cannabis Sales Tax and Excise Tax Revenue.
The Maine Mayors Coalition is a nonpartisan group representing the mayors of eleven Maine communities - Auburn, Bangor, Biddeford, Lewiston, Portland, Rockland, Saco, Sanford, South Portland, Waterville and Westbrook - and nearly 300,000 residents. The Coalition advocates on behalf of our citizens and municipalities for policies that recognize the vital services Maine cities provide and the positive impact Maine cities have on our state. The Coalition seeks to work in partnership with state and federal elected officials to meet the needs of Maine people.
Cities permitting adult use cannabis establishments will benefit under both bills. LD 177 directs 10 percent of the funds in the Adult Use Cannabis Public Health and Safety and Municipal Opt-in Fund go equally to these municipalities. LD 347 establishes a new fund requiring 12 percent of the revenue from sales and excise taxes on adult use cannabis be distributed to the municipalities.
Like you, we make every effort to keep property taxes as low as possible while providing our citizens with necessary municipal services. Rising costs and spiking property values in recent years have made this much more difficult. And, it is Maine property owners who pay the price with higher property taxes.
The new income streams included in both bills will provide our cities with additional financial resources that will help us meet our municipal obligations. In turn, our homeowners and businesses would see property tax relief through a reduction in the municipal tax levy.
We respectfully ask you to support LD 177 and LD 347. Thank you for your time.

Senator Hickman, Representative Supica and distinguished members of the Veterans and Legal Affairs Committee, my name is Debbie Laurie and I am the City Manager of Bangor. I am providing testimony today on behalf of the City of Bangor in support of LD 347, An Act to Provide Qualifying Municipalities a Percentage of Adult Use Cannabis Sales Tax and Excise Tax Revenue.
As a service center community, Bangor is a vital local, regional and statewide economic engine that provides access to educational, employment, retail, professional, medical and social services not available in other locales. We are home to 15 Adult Use Cannabis establishments. All of which contribute to the broad based sales and excise tax revenue collected by the state.
The Legislature and the City Council face similar budgetary challenges: increasing costs, flat or declining revenues, compliance with mandates, strategic investments in the future, increasing calls for service, etc. While the State's revenue streams are broad, at the municipal level our primary revenue stream remains limited to property taxes. With the plethora of bills under consideration in the coming session, it is clear that one of our shared priorities for the coming year is property tax relief.
The Legislature found that the principal problem of financing municipal services is the burden on the property tax, and that to stabilize the municipal property tax burden and to aid in financing all municipal services, it is necessary to provide funds from the broad-based taxes of the State.
The City of Bangor believes LD 347 is another means by which the state can share taxes generated within its communities within those communities to help directly relieve the property tax burden and to strengthen the State and local partnership.
On behalf of the Bangor City Council, I urge you to pass LD 347 to alleviate the property tax burden on our residents.
Thank you for your consideration, and please do not hesitate to reach out with questions.

February 12, 2025
Senator Hickman, Representative Supica and distinguished members of the Veterans and Legal Affairs
Committee, my name is Elizabeth Caruso. I live in Caratunk, and I represent House District 72 representing 9 towns and 20 townships and unorganized territories of northern Somerset County. I am providing testimony in support of LD 347.
I have served the Town of Caratunk as the selectboard chair for the last 19 years, having been first elected in 2006
as the First Selectman. In 2022, I was also elected to the Maine Municipal Association's Legislative Policy Committee to represent the 36 towns of Senate District 5. Throughout these years of municipal service, I have become acquainted with the day-to-day logistical operations as well as the uniqueness of Maine's varying municipal operations based on geographies and populations. Cannabis operations within municipalities have been a hot topic for some time.
Caratunk's legislative body, following a moratorium, enacted a Marijuana Ordinance in 2017 which prohibited
retail operations. The reasons were varied: we are remotely rural; our municipal officers are all part-time and work other jobs; and absent present/local law enforcement, we completely rely on the limited staffing of the
county sheriff department and/or even less present state police. I explain this all to affirm my support of this bill
which only sends revenue sharing to towns that opt-in to cannabis operations.
However, there are many rural towns that took a different approach and allowed retail Cannabis operations, and
therefore, must navigate issues around zoning, permitting, public infrastructure, public safety, etc. Whether their
municipal offices are staffed part-time or full-time, whether they are rural or urban, whether they have their own
code enforcement officer or share a CEO with other towns (such as Caratunk does), or whether they have local
law enforcement or must coordinate with the county, all municipalities have to navigate retail Cannabis operations successfillly, effectively, and safely.
Municipalities with Cannabis operations in their jurisdiction are tasked with evaluating, permitting and approving
site locations, yearly monitoring (including on-premise visits by the CEO and fire chiefs), license renewals, filling
out town portions of the state license renewals, and all related correspondences within the town in regards to the Cannabis operations. Compensating towns that opt-in by providing proportional revenue sharing does not only make sense, but it encourages participation while supporting a safer and healthier industry.
Municipal officers juggle a lot, and Cannabis consumes time that could be used on other activities. I support LD
347 because it directly compensates the very municipalities which allow this industry to exist, but the compensation is in a manner and measure proportional to where the Cannabis revenue is generated.
Thank you for the opportunity to share and for your careful consideration of the local government perspective
Proudly Serving House District 72

Testimony of Mayor Mark Dion of the City of Portland In Support of
LD 347, An Act to Provide Qualifying Municipalities a Percentage of Adult Use Cannabis Sales Tax and Excise Tax Revenue
Senator Hickman, Representative Supica and members of the Veterans and Legal Affairs Committee, I am Mayor Mark Dion, and I am providing testimony in support of LD 347 on behalf of the City of Portland. Nearly 70,000 Mainers call Portland home, though many more than that come to Portland each day to work, and for purposes of this discussion, there are thirty retail adult use establishments in Portland as well as additional adult use cultivation, manufacturing, and testing facilities in the City.
LD 347 establishes a new fund requiring 12 percent of the revenue from sales and excise taxes on adult use cannabis be distributed to the municipalities. The City of Portland supports LD 347 because while additional the proceeds to each municipality that allows adult use cannabis establishment would be modest, this proposal represents an important step towards sharing a greater portion of cannabis revenue with municipalities who have opted in to allow such businesses within their borders and are incurring significant expenditures related to licensing and enforcement.
In Portland, opting in to allow cannabis businesses means we have also taken on zoning, permitting, and public safety connected to these new establishments, among other duties. These duties require resources, yet under the current system, Portland does not receive a direct allocation of the tax from the revenue these businesses help to generate. We have been pleased to have cannabis establishments in Portland, but the energy and pace of growth in a new industry also have the capacity to stress the city's operations and the State's existing system of municipal revenue sharing does not include any factor for the volume of cannabis establishments within a municipality's borders.
As others have already testified, it would be fair for the City to receive some of the revenue from the cannabis industry and it is also necessary for the City to continue to help regulate and support the industry, meet all of our City obligations, and attempt to keep property taxes in check. Sharing a portion of the revenue generated in Portland would provide financial support for law enforcement, essential regulation, public health initiatives, and community programs.

TESTIMONY OF MICHAEL J. ALLEN, ASSOCIATE COMMISSIONER FOR TAX POLICY
DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE AND FINANCIAL SERVICES
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Veterans and Legal Affairs Hearing Date: February 12, 2025, Wednesday, at 11:00 AM
LD 347 - "An Act to Provide Qualifying Municipalities a Percentage of Adult Use Cannabis Sales Tax and Excise Tax Revenue"
Senator Hickman, Representative Supica, and members of the Veterans and Legal Affairs Committee - good morning, my name is Michael Allen, Associate Commissioner for Tax Policy in the Department of Administrative and Financial Services. I am testifying at the request of the Administration Against LD 347, "An Act to Provide Qualifying Municipalities a Percentage of Adult Use Cannabis Sales Tax and Excise Tax Revenue."
This bill creates new revenue-sharing for municipalities that have allowed cannabis establishments within the municipality by establishing the Local Government Cannabis Revenue Fund, funded by a monthly transfer of 12% of the sales and excise tax receipts from sales and transfers of adult use cannabis and adult use cannabis products. Revenues would be distributed in proportion to the amount of "state revenues generated by" cannabis establishments in each municipality.
Though possibly overlooked, municipalities already receive a 5% share of both adult use and medical cannabis sales tax revenues simply as a function of the general Revenue Sharing formula base consisting of 5% of State Government's total monthly sales, corporate and personal income tax revenues. Via general Revenue Sharing, municipalities also are already receiving a share of the corporate
1

and individual income tax revenues paid by cannabis business owners and employees.
It should be noted that Part F of the Governor's biennial budget (LD 210) includes a proposal to reduce the current transfer to the Adult Use Cannabis Public Health and Safety and Municipal Opt-in Fund of adult use cannabis sales and excise tax, from 12% to 9% of receipts, in inverse proportion to the additional revenue that would be generated by the proposed increase in the adult use cannabis sales tax from 10% to 14%. This bill would run counter to and more than offset the Governor's budget proposal by reducing General Fund revenue by an estimated $6 million per year.
Turning to technical language concerns:
� The language in Section 1 of the bill, proposed Title 28-B, Section 407, subsection 3, should be clarified to only include the sources of the Local Government Cannabis Revenue Fund as identified in subsection 2.
� Section 2 of the bill should be amended on lines 31 and 36 to read: "received . . . pursuant to section 1811, subsection 1, paragraph D, subparagraph (5)."
� To facilitate the transfers directed by this bill in coordination with the current transfers to the Adult Use Cannabis Public Health and Safety and Municipal Opt-in Fund and the Local Government Fund, LD 347 should include language specifying the timing and calculation of the transfers in relation to each other.
� Maine Revenue Services would be required to update its tax processing system to determine distribution amounts, meaning a general effective date (90 days post-adjournment) may be too soon for
2

implementation. The bill should also include a start date for transfers to the Local Government Cannabis Revenue Fund, preferably on the first day of a month. � The bill requires the Treasurer to "retain the actual costs of administering the fund." A simpler approach would be determining a fixed monthly amount to be retained instead. Finally, with respect to smaller communities with only one or a few affected businesses, the reporting and redistribution of revenues as specified in the bill may indirectly allow greater public knowledge of tax data of those businesses that otherwise would be confidential. The Administration looks forward to working with the Committee on the bill; representatives from MRS will be here for the Work Session to provide additional information and respond in detail to the Committee's questions.

Senator Hickman, Representative Supica and esteemed members of the Joint Standing Committee on Veterans and Legal Affairs, the Maine Service Centers Coalition is submitting testimony in support of LD 177, An Act to Create Municipal Cannabis Revenue Sharing, and LD 347, An Act to Provide Qualifying Municipalities a Percentage of Adult Use Cannabis Sales Tax and Excise Tax Revenue.
The Maine Service Centers Coalition, comprised of 26 towns and cities across the state, articulates the importance of healthy and thriving service center communities, advocates for public policy that supports and contributes to the economic and social viability of our communities, and collaborates with municipal officials, legislators, state agencies and non-profits to pursue quality of life for all who live and work in our state.
We are supporting LD 177 and LD 347 as both provide welcome sources of funding for cities and towns with adult use cannabis establishments. Under LD 177, these municipalities would receive 10 percent of the Adult Use Cannabis Public Health and Safety and Municipal Opt-in Fund. For these reasons, we ask you to give every consideration to supporting LD 177 and LD 347.

10032774:
Testimony of the Maine Municipal Association
In Support of
LD 177 - An Act to Create Municipal Cannabis Revenue Sharing & LD 347 - An Act to Provide Qualifying Municipalities a Percentage of Adult Use Cannabis Sales Tax and Excise Tax Revenue
February 12, 2025
Senator Hickman, Representative Supica and members of the Veterans and Legal Affairs Committee, my name is Rebecca Lambert, and I am providing testimony in support of LD 177 and LD 347 on behalf of the Maine Municipal Association's (MMA) elected 70-member Legislative Policy Committee (LPC). For reference, the LPC guides MMA's advocacy efforts and establishes positions on bills of municipal interest.
Municipal officials express strong support for both LD 177 and LD 347 aimed to share a greater portion of cannabis revenue with municipalities who have opted in to allow these businesses within their jurisdictions. They appreciate the recognition and would only suggest disbursing the shared revenue proportionally among the municipalities where the revenue was generated.
When Maine voters approved cannabis legalization, the intent was to create a regulated market that benefits the state and local communities. Municipalities that have opted in to allow cannabis businesses have taken on the responsibilities of zoning, permitting, law enforcement coordination, and public safety oversight, among other duties. These responsibilities require resources, yet under the current system, many of these municipalities do not receive a direct share, except the portion distributed through the traditional revenue sharing program, of the revenue they helped to generate. Local leaders feel it is both fair and necessary to ensure that local governments receive a portion of the revenue generated by the industry they help regulate and support.
Cannabis revenue sharing, in any manner, would provide much-needed financial support for local infrastructure, law enforcement, public health initiatives, and community programs. It would also incentivize more municipalities to participate in the legal cannabis market, expanding access to regulated and tested products while reducing the prevalence of illicit sales. Fair revenue distribution strengthens local economies and ensures the sustainability of Maine's cannabis industry.
Across the country where cannabis legalization has occurred, local governments who have opted into the program have seen the benefit from a portion of the tax revenue. For example, Nevada dedicates 15% of tax revenue to local governments, Massachusetts and California provide for a local option sales tax to be imposed, and in Michigan, 15% of the excise tax is earmarked for county government, with an additional 15% for municipalities--equating to a nearly $10 million dollar investment in municipal and county governments.
LD 177 and LD 347 have the potential to create a more equitable system that benefits both the state and the communities that make this industry possible. Thank you for your commitment to ensuring a fair and sustainable future for Maine's cannabis industry and the municipalities who support it. I appreciate your time and consideration of the municipal perspective.
